title: CNN, Politico, and MS NOW Sue Trump After White House Ban
summary:
What would happen if you were kicked out of a place just for saying something the person in charge didn't like? That's what three news organizations say happened to them at the White House.

CNN, Politico, and MS NOW — all news companies — were told on Friday they could no longer come into the White House. President Donald Trump accused them of writing "fiction or lies" about his team. On Saturday, their reporters were denied access to the building.

On Monday, the three companies sued the Trump administration in court. They want a judge to quickly rule that the ban is unconstitutional — meaning it breaks the rules in the U.S. Constitution. They said they are defending "the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports."

The First Amendment is a rule in the U.S. Constitution that says the government cannot limit what the press writes. Courts have usually said this means the government can't punish news groups for what they report.

After the ban, five major TV networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC — said they would stop sharing their White House coverage. That means when Trump travels, there might be no regular TV crew following him. On Monday, CNN's booth inside the White House was empty, with screens turned off. Instead, a CNN crew reported from a public sidewalk outside.

Trump posted on Truth Social that he was not attacking the free press, but targeting "FAKE NEWS."
why_it_matters: If the government could kick out reporters it doesn't like, people — including kids — would only hear one side of the story, so it matters who gets to ask questions and share the news.

background_read: The First Amendment (part of the U.S. Constitution, the country's most important set of rules) says the government cannot make laws that stop the press from writing what it wants.
The White House (the building in Washington where the U.S. president lives and works) normally lets a group of reporters come inside every day to ask the president questions and share what happens.

There is an old argument about this: news groups say the government must never punish them for what they report, while presidents say they can choose who is allowed inside their own building. U.S. courts have often sided with the news groups.

WHERE: The White House in Washington — CNN's booth inside sat empty with its screens turned off, so a CNN crew reported from a public sidewalk outside.
WHY: The companies say they are defending 'the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports,' which they say the First Amendment protects.
